threat_assessment:
The table sees a four-mana Wizard, a fistful of Elves, and 36 Forests. Their read: fair stompy deck, ramping politely, no combo — and the record agrees with them. Zero contained combos, no game changers, a bracket floor of 1 against a target of 3. On paper you are the most ignorable deck at the table. Keep it that way. That paper is your camouflage, and your whole early game is spent keeping it accurate.

Your interaction is the untapped Forest. Stack 001 is the engine: Radagast's discount-and-flash resets every turn, so a four-player round hands you four windows and Wood Elves costs one green mana on an opponent's end step. So stop tapping out. Two open green is Frostfang, or Heroic Intervention, or nothing at all, and the table must price all three (strategy:multiplayer.pod-management). The card they cannot see does the deterrence work — your job is only to hold it back and pass.

Spring the first trap early and make it cheap for you, expensive for them. Stack 002 is the lesson plan: Frostfang flashed after blockers are declared turns damage already lined up into deathtouch, and one unblocked 1/1 pays you two cards on the way out. A player who loses two attackers to open mana stops attacking you for the rest of the night. That is the point of the trade — you are not buying creatures, you are buying a reputation.

Three signals flip you from ignored to archenemy, and you control all three. A fifth body — because everyone can count to Craterhoof. A visible finisher — Chord of Calling mana held up with a big board is an announcement, so do not hold eleven mana ostentatiously unless you intend to use it. And Selvala — she actually reads friendly, since she offers everyone draws; let them believe it, and do not lead her into open removal without a reason, because she is your only card of her class and the sim finds her in barely one game in six.

Do not pivot at four bodies. Stack 003 did the arithmetic: Craterhoof over four other bodies is 36 unblocked into one seat — loud, board-committing, and not lethal from 40. The fifth body clears the bar. The count is the trigger (strategy:pivot-point): five bodies plus a finisher in hand, and not before. A telegraphed pivot that falls four short is how a deflection deck elects itself archenemy for free.

Be honest about your own clock. The sim measures 3.35 bodies by turn six and the finisher in hand 43% of the time — both floors, since it models neither the discount nor a single flash cast, but respect the shape: your pivot is usually not ready on turn six, so do not start acting like the threat on turn five. Every turn you look like the ramp deck running slightly behind, someone else eats the removal.

And when the count is right, embrace it completely. Flash the last body in on the end step before your turn — stack 001's window works the same for a giant as for Wood Elves — untap, and point everything at the seat that can rebuild interaction fastest, with Heroic Intervention or Tyvar's Stand held for the vote you just called. There is no radar to be under once the Behemoth resolves, and you do not need one: you counted, they didn't. Four verified stacks and ten thousand goldfish runs say the plan is sound — now go play the games that prove it.
matchups:
Sort the table by one question: who can afford to ignore your open mana? The seats that can't will slow down and play worse (strategy:information). The seats that can are the ones these notes are for.

The flier deck is your worst axis, so say it out loud in your head and plan around it: one reach body in the whole 99 — Old Fat Spider — and nothing else that blocks the sky. Do not plan to block. Race. Hold Warg Tactics and Unforgiving Aim for the one flier that actually outraces you — the commander, the engine dragon — never the first bird that chips you. Pick Your Poison's flying mode makes each opponent sacrifice a flier of their choice, so fire it only when their best flier is their only flier. Meanwhile the ground is wide open in both directions: keep Toski and Frostfang connecting, and make the sky find its last points before your five bodies find theirs.

Against aggro you are the control seat (strategy:whos-the-beatdown). Stack 002 already wrote the sign on your lawn — attack here and everything you lined up dies to a flashed Frostfang. Show it once, then let two open Forests do the job the card used to. Radagast's 2/5 blocks the early turns for free, and Guardian Augmenter flashes in to make him a hexproof 4/7 the moment someone tries to break the wall. Let the aggro seat spend itself into the other two players, then pivot the turn you stabilize — every passive turn past stable is a free draw step for somebody else (strategy:pivot-point).

Against sweeper control, fear the wrath early and welcome it late — the crossover card is Fecundity. Before your engines land, commit exactly as much board as wins before the sweeper arrives and not one body more (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math). After Fecundity, the math flips: stack 004 verified that a Day of Judgment over your board pays you a card per creature — four wakes for you against their one — while Toski stands there indestructible and even Radagast's death is seen before he leaves for the command zone. Your rebuild is a feature, not a scramble: Radagast's first recast is six mana in a deck that finds ramp by turn six in 92% of runs, so redeploy worst-first, hold the finisher for their second sweeper, and flash the rebuild on end steps where a sorcery-speed wrath can never quite catch it.

Against combo you are the beatdown, full stop — you lose every long game against inevitability (strategy:whos-the-beatdown). The toolkit is three items: the clock, Collector Ouphe, and Veil of Summer. Flash Ouphe in through Radagast's window on the combo player's own turn — stack 001 says the discount and the flash are live there — and hold Veil for the turn they point removal at Ouphe or disruption at your hand. Then be honest about the clock: stack 003 says one alpha strike takes one seat, not three, so the moment their proximity beats every board in sight, rank them archenemy (strategy:threat-assessment) and point all five bodies at the combo player, not the open one.

Against the artifact table you get to be the tax collector. Collector Ouphe switches off every activated mana rock at the table while your 36 Forests never notice he exists. Boseiju, Who Endures kills the key piece from your hand, and Life from the Loam brings it back — dredge Loam off any of your constant draw triggers, return Boseiju, channel again, with the cost shrinking for each legendary creature you control until it is one green mana per shot. Add Caustic Caterpillar, Wickerbough Elder, and Nantuko Vigilante as bodies that double as answers, and their engine pays you rent every turn it tries to restart. That is nine removal-class cards pointed at the one table that must respect all of them — collect.
